strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated practical problem in professional poster design with fine-grained font control
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (SkyReels, AnyText, IAM, CVL) with consistent SOTA results (85.36% English Sen. Acc., 77.10% Chinese on AnyText)
Practical innovation: reference glyph patches enable zero-shot font transfer without explicit font labels or inference-time fine-tuning
Well-designed data curation strategy with content-style decoupling pipeline, dual verification (OCR + DINO), and 100k high-quality samples
VLM-based OCR adaptation effectively handles ornamental/calligraphic fonts that standard OCR methods fail on
Strong empirical improvements on key metrics: FID 6.12 vs 13.85 (FLUX-Text), LPIPS 0.0246 vs 0.0729 on English
Text-region weighted loss is simple but effective for addressing class imbalance in poster editing
Solid ablation studies validating Font Style Reference and weighted loss contribution
Practical inference optimization achieving 10× speedup via distillation while maintaining quality
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily fine-tuning existing model (Qwen-Image-Edit) with dual-stream VAE concatenation (straightforward) and simple spatial loss reweighting
Serious reproducibility barriers: relies on proprietary models (Qwen-Image-Edit, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-8B), proprietary data generation, in-house 100k dataset, no public code or dataset release mentioned
Small in-house benchmark (200 samples) insufficient for establishing SOTA claims; lacks dataset statistics, split information, and representativeness analysis

Incomplete technical clarity: glyph reference map generation (Xg) not well-explained; mechanism for handling multiple regions with different fonts simultaneously unclear; LoRA fine-tuning details sparse
Significant accuracy-style trade-off inadequately discussed: FSR increases DINO 17.8% but decreases NED 2.3%; explanation why style requires degraded accuracy is cursory
Problematic evaluation metrics: DINO captures content structure as well as style (not style-only); B-PSNR poorly correlates with perceptual quality; no user study validating designer satisfaction
Handwritten text claims misleadingly framed: zero-shot results on untrained domain presented as strength without clear context; not uniformly better than baselines in Table 3
Incremental improvements over strong baseline: +2.44% over Qwen-Image-Edit alone (82.92% → 85.36%); SOTA advantage may be dataset-specific rather than methodological
Missing critical ablations: VAE freezing justification, reference patch size/quality sensitivity, number of patches needed, comparison of feature injection methods
No failure case analysis or discussion of limitations: method robustness on long text, unusual scripts (Arabic, Devanagari), extreme scales, textured backgrounds unexplored
Practical details underspecified: absolute inference latency not reported (only relative speedup); computational requirements for practitioners not discussed
Writing quality issues: typo in abstract ('handwrittent'), Figure 3 unclear, repetitive sections between introduction and related work

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem in professional design workflows with a pragmatic solution using reference glyph patches
Comprehensive dataset contributions (SkyReels-OCR 40K and 100K paired decoupled dataset) with rigorous multi-stage curation
Strong experimental results with consistent improvements across multiple metrics (Semantic Accuracy 83.34%, NED 0.9502) on diverse benchmarks
Extensive evaluation including user studies, ablation studies, and multilingual capability demonstrations
Achieves effective simultaneous control of text content and font style, a key practical requirement
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and thorough supplementary material
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily combines existing components (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen-Image-Edit, standard VAE) with straightforward modifications
Overstated 'zero-shot' claims - using reference glyph patches is few-shot learning; sensitivity to reference glyph quality not analyzed
Modest improvements over some baselines (e.g., B-PSNR 34.17 vs 34.33 for Calligrapher); not always clear why improvements are significant
Proprietary SkyReels-Text benchmark limits independent verification; dataset sourced from filtered Pinterest/Amazon with potential selection bias
Incomplete technical details: VAE architecture specs, data preprocessing thresholds, hyperparameter sensitivity (λ=5 choice), and inference time comparisons lacking
Minimal failure mode analysis - paper doesn't clearly characterize when/why method struggles or its generalization boundaries
Content-style decoupling relies on ad-hoc heuristics (20% character overlap, quality thresholds) without sufficient ablation studies
Limited multilingual and script diversity evaluation - only English/Chinese tested; generalization to non-Latin and complex scripts unclear
Reproducibility concerns - dataset proprietary with copyright restrictions; code availability dependent on publication; Qwen model version dependencies
User study limited in scale (4 competitors) and some baseline comparisons are against methods designed for different tasks

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem in font-aware text editing for design applications
Proposes a clever visual conditioning strategy using reference glyph patches that eliminates font label requirements
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including user studies and ablation studies with competitive quantitative results
Contributes two potentially valuable datasets (SkyReels-OCR-40K and content-style decoupled dataset) with careful curation
Demonstrates practical capabilities on challenging scenarios including small-size text, multi-font, and zero-shot handwritten text generation
Well-structured paper with extensive supplementary material and clear presentation of the pipeline
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty for CVPR: primarily combines existing components (VAE, Qwen2.5-VL, MMDIT+LoRA) with straightforward reference patch conditioning rather than introducing novel methods or theory
Primary evaluation relies on authors' proprietary dataset (SkyReels-OCR-40K); limited evaluation on established public benchmarks; raises generalization concerns

Incomplete reproducibility: no code availability stated, dataset release plan unclear, missing implementation details (training procedures, hyperparameter selection justification for λ=5), inference time unreported

Evaluation methodology concerns: OCR-based metrics don't capture typographic perceptual quality; LPIPS/FID poorly suited for text quality; Table 2 contains inconsistencies in reported performance comparisons
Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic discussion of failure cases, font-type limitations, or sensitivity to reference glyph quality; only qualitative examples provided
Limited scope: specialized for poster design with unclear generalization; requires high-quality reference images; only English and Chinese evaluated; zero-shot handwritten results only qualitative
Questionable dataset construction choices: VLM-based annotation potential bias, arbitrary threshold choices (20% overlap for divergent text, ≤50% for 'Effective Text') lack justification
Fairness concerns in comparisons: several baseline methods not designed for font-aware editing; missing recent 2024-2025 text editing methods in comparison

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in fine-grained font-controllable text editing with an intuitive reference glyph patch approach
Novel dual-stream visual conditioning mechanism that effectively decouples textual content from typographic style
State-of-the-art performance on poster design task (83.34% Sen. Acc., improving over baselines with comprehensive metrics)
Exceptional dataset creation effort: SkyReels-OCR-40K with rigorous multi-step curation and content-style decoupled dataset with 100K samples
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (SkyReels-Text, AnyText, IAM, CVL) with complementary evaluation metrics
Thorough ablation studies clearly demonstrating the contribution of key components (Table 4)
Strong practical performance: handles complex scenarios (multi-font, small text, paragraph-level editing) across English and Chinese
User preference study confirming practical superiority over commercial and academic baselines
Good reproducibility: clear implementation details, promised code release, and transparent methodology
weaknesses: Limited scope: framework is specifically tuned for poster design with unclear generalization to other document types, signage, or varied backgrounds
Handwritten text evaluation concerns: zero-shot evaluation on IAM/CVL without explicit training is not well-justified, and claims of 'highly realistic' generation are overstated
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing recent diffusion-based text editing methods and some cited approaches (e.g., DiffUTE)
Technical clarity gaps: glyph patch extraction details underspecified, insufficient discussion of handling out-of-distribution fonts, and MMDIT block modifications lack architectural detail
Inference efficiency not explored: no runtime analysis, computational cost comparisons, or discussion of practical deployment considerations
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; some improvements are marginal (83.34% vs 82.88%)
Limited failure case analysis: minimal discussion of failure modes, edge cases (extremely long text, very small fonts), or when the method breaks down
Evaluation metric concerns: Spatial IoU may not capture perceptual quality universally, and DINO similarity could reflect feature overfitting rather than quality
Limited script diversity: only English and Chinese evaluated; claims of multilingual capability unsupported by diverse script evaluation
Dataset domain bias: SkyReels-OCR-40K is poster-specific and content-style decoupling uses relatively simple manipulation strategies
